query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) intended for high-temperature applications, the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance is governed by the uniform elemental distribution that minimizes local depletion of key oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr, Al). This uniformity, stemming from high configurational entropy, promotes the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale that more effectively resists spallation and excessive growth compared to non‐HEA systems with similar overall composition.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a well-mixed, homogeneous microstructure and controlled amounts of oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr, Al) prepared under conditions ensuring high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of materials: one set with conventional processing yielding a more segregated (low-entropy) microstructure (but with similar overall composition) and the HEA with uniform elemental distribution. Subject both to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation (e.g., 900–1100°C) in an oxygen-rich environment over a predefined duration, ensuring the same thermal exposure and oxygen partial pressure for both sample sets.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform distribution of oxide-forming elements in the HEA microstructure, as contrasted with possible elemental clustering or depletion in conventional alloys.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous dispersion of key elements. This uniformity enables a steady, continuous supply of oxide-forming elements to the surface, promoting the rapid development of a dense and adherent protective oxide scale with self-healing characteristics. In contrast, in alloys with segregated microstructures, local depletion leads to discontinuous oxide scale formation and faster degradation under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA is expected to form a thinner, more uniform, and adherent protective oxide layer with reduced spallation and slower overall oxidation kinetics compared to the conventional alloy with a segregated structure.
generation.baseline: The conventional alloy of similar overall composition but lacking the uniform, high-entropy derived microstructure, which is expected to form a less uniform and more rapidly growing oxide scale, leading to poorer oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable within high-temperature oxidation conditions where diffusion processes govern oxide scale formation, and it assumes the presence of sufficient oxide-forming elements (such as Cr or Al) in both alloy systems. It may not fully apply under extreme conditions (e.g., very high or cyclic thermal stresses) that lead to aggressive oxide spallation regardless of microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., exact reduction in oxide scale thickness or oxidation rate) is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition, processing conditions, and test environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct controlled high-temperature oxidation tests on two groups: one group composed of HEAs with a confirmed uniform microstructure and another group of conventionally processed alloys with similar overall composition but known microstructural segregation. Monitor the evolution of the oxide scale using in situ high-temperature microscopy, post-test cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for compositional mapping, and measure oxidation kinetics via weight gain analysis.
measurements: Oxidation kinetics (thermogravimetric analysis for weight gain over time)
Adherence of oxide layer (spallation tests under thermal cycling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not exhibit a significantly more uniform, thinner, and adherent oxide scale with slower oxidation kinetics compared to the conventional alloy—i.e., if both material groups show similar oxide layer characteristics and degradation rates under identical conditions—then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy governs the superior development and retention of a protective oxide layer is falsified.
